title: Module & Provider Stability Plan: compatibility map and pinning strategy for private VPC IaC
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: Produce a canonical compatibility map and conservative version pinning policy for Terraform CLI, providers and Redwood IaC modules that we use for VPC/private deployments. This ticket captures the matrix of tested combinations, the recommended pin syntax for module releases and provider blocks, an automated CI gate and a staged upgrade playbook with health checks and rollback steps. The intent is to reduce upgrade incidents during Private (VPC) deployment upgrades and support predictable customer upgrades and on-prem bundles.
acceptance_criteria: Compatibility matrix published as a single source-of-truth in the Private IaC repo
CI gate fails on Terraform plan if provider/module versions are outside approved ranges
Automated test runs (terraform init/plan/apply-dry) for at least 3 representative stacks succeed under the pinned combos
Runbook for staged upgrades (canary, cohort, full) documented with health checks and rollback steps
A migration checklist and deprecation notes for any pinned-to-unpinned transitions
matrix_summary: Terraform CLI: supported 1.5.x (recommended 1.5.7) and 1.6.x (allowed), pin in CI to exact binary used for plan/apply

hashicorp/aws provider: approved range 4.60.0 - 4.99.x, recommended pin: "~> 4.60, >= 4.60.0" for modules that rely on new resource arguments; for top-level deployments use explicit <=4.99.99 upper bound
hashicorp/tls: allowed 2.x and 3.x depending on module consumer; recommended pin per-module, default "~> 3.0"
registry.redwood/vpc module (rwinf/vpc/aws): tested with aws provider 4.60 - 4.88; recommended module major v2 with minor pins, example module source = "rwinf/vpc/aws?ref=v2.7.1"
registry.redwood/k8s-provisioner (rwinf/k8s): tested with aws 4.70 - 4.88 and kubernetes provider 2.20 - 2.24; pin module to v1.4.x for clusters created before 2024 and v1.5.x for current clusters
third-party modules (VPC peering, VPN): audit required before bumping provider versions; default to vendor-pinned refs in our forked modules
steps: 1) Inventory: run script to enumerate all module sources and provider constraints across private-infra/* and stacks/*
2) Test matrix build: create ephemeral CI jobs to init/plan using each matrix row (Terraform binary X provider Y module Z)
3) Approve ranges: capture failing cells and either adjust module code or narrow provider constraints
4) Update modules: publish module patch releases with explicit compatibility notes and examples
5) CI enforcement: add a pre-merge hook that validates version constraints against approved ranges
6) Canaries: perform a canary stack upgrade in staging and then a single low-risk customer cohort in prod
7) Monitor & rollback: use health checks; if thresholds breached, run automated rollback procedure
ci_checks: Terraform-version check: lock CI to exact TF binary used for the compatibility job
Provider-constraint lint: fail if provider source or version ranges are not in the approved list
Module-ref check: ensure module refs use tags (ref=vX.Y.Z) not branch names
Plan-diff smoke tests: run terraform plan and compare a known-good baseline to detect breaking provider changes
Integration smoke: apply to ephemeral account with minimal resources and run post-provision health probes
rollback_plan: If canary fails, stop the rollout and revert the module/provider versions in the stack repo to prior commit via automated PR
Run terraform apply with previous statefile and previous module refs; verify networking and control-plane endpoints are restored
If rollback apply fails, escalate to on-call infra lead and run manual resources remediation checklist
Notify affected customers and set a retrospective meeting to capture root cause and mitigation
health_checks: API connectivity: confirm control plane endpoints respond (200) from three regions
Networking smoke: verify inter-subnet communication and route tables for canary VPCs
Service checks: K8s API server health, bootstrap jobs completed, nodes Ready within expected time
Cost & quota: monitor for unexpected increases in instance counts or failed provisioning due to provider changes
Alerting: ensure SLOs for provisioning success rate and time-to-ready are within thresholds; trigger rollback if breached
notes: Key trade-offs: tighter pins reduce risk of silent provider upgrades causing drift, but increase maintenance cost for bump cadence. We recommend conservative upper bounds for provider majors and explicit module refs for all published modules. For third-party modules we will maintain forks with pinned refs until we certify upstream releases.
